claim: Mouse CBY1 interactors were identified by LAP-Tag affinity purification using IMCD3 cells stably expressing CBY1 fused to the EGFP-TEV-S peptide tag.
source: We initially identified mouse CBY1 interactors by LAP-Tag affinity purification using IMCD3 cells (murine Inner Medullary Collecting Duct cells) stably expressing CBY1 fused to the EGFP-TEV-S peptide tag (see Materials and methods section).
evidence: The manuscript describes the experimental method used to identify CBY1 interactors, which is a direct experimental observation.

claim: Analysis of LAP-CBY1 complex revealed the presence of DZIP1 and FAM92 among 22 identified proteins.
source: Analysis of LAP-CBY1 complex revealed the presence of DZIP1 and FAM92 among 22 identified proteins (see full list in Supplementary file 1), in agreement with recently published data (Li et al., 2016b; Breslow et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript reports experimental results from mass spectrometry analysis and cites supporting literature.

claim: DZIP1/1L and FAM92a/b each show a unique ortholog gene in Drosophila, CG13617 and CG6405 respectively.
source: DZIP1/1L and FAM92a/b each show a unique ortholog gene in Drosophila, CG13617 and CG6405 respectively (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), but are absent, like CBY1, from the C. elegans genome.
evidence: The manuscript presents phylogenetic analysis data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Drosophila Dzip1 and Fam92 each interact with Cby.
source: By co-immunoprecipitating Cby-GFP and HA-Dzip1 or HA-Fam92, we demonstrate that Drosophila Dzip1 and Fam92, each interact with Cby (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript describes co-immunoprecipitation experiments demonstrating protein-protein interactions.

claim: Dzip1 or Fam92 do not apparently interact with each other in co-IP experiments.
source: Dzip1 or Fam92 do not apparently interact with each other in these co-IP experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript reports negative results from co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: When all three proteins are expressed together, immunoprecipitation of GFP-Dzip1 pulls down both Cby and Fam92.
source: However, when all three proteins are expressed together, immunoprecipitation of GFP-Dzip1 pulls down both Cby and Fam92, suggesting that all three proteins are present in one complex when co-expressed in mammalian cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript describes co-immunoprecipitation results showing complex formation.

claim: All three proteins (Dzip1, Fam92, and Cby) are present in one complex when co-expressed in mammalian cells.
source: However, when all three proteins are expressed together, immunoprecipitation of GFP-Dzip1 pulls down both Cby and Fam92, suggesting that all three proteins are present in one complex when co-expressed in mammalian cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: The manuscript infers complex formation from co-immunoprecipitation data.

claim: dzip1 and fam92 are exclusively expressed in the two kinds of Drosophila ciliated cell types, namely type I sensory neurons and male germ cells.
source: We determined that both dzip1 and fam92 are exclusively expressed in the two kinds of Drosophila ciliated cell types, namely type I sensory neurons and male germ cells (Figures 1 and 2).
evidence: The manuscript reports expression pattern analysis using transgenic reporter flies.

claim: Type I sensory neurons comprise chordotonal (Ch) and external sensory (ES) neurons, which harbor motile and immotile cilia respectively.
source: Type I sensory neurons comprise chordotonal (Ch) and external sensory (ES) neurons, which harbor motile and immotile cilia respectively (Figure 1A) (Gogendeau and Basto, 2010; Jana et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about sensory neuron types and their cilia.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 decorate the base of the cilia at the tip of the sensory dendrites.
source: Dzip1 and Fam92 decorate the base of the cilia at the tip of the sensory dendrites (labeled with 22C10) (Figure 1B, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence localization data.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 co-localize with Cby in sensory neurons.
source: By performing, super-resolution 3D structured-illumination microscopy (3D-SIM), we confirmed that Dzip1 and Fam92 co-localize with Cby in sensory neurons (Figure 1C), demonstrating their restricted localization at the ciliary transition zone.
evidence: The manuscript reports super-resolution microscopy data showing protein co-localization.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 have restricted localization at the ciliary transition zone.
source: By performing, super-resolution 3D structured-illumination microscopy (3D-SIM), we confirmed that Dzip1 and Fam92 co-localize with Cby in sensory neurons (Figure 1C), demonstrating their restricted localization at the ciliary transition zone.
evidence: The manuscript infers transition zone localization from co-localization with known TZ marker Cby.

claim: In spermatocytes, centrioles have a specific behavior as both mother and daughter centrioles of each pair elongate and dock to the plasma membrane.
source: In the male germline, Dzip1 and Fam92 appear first in spermatocytes (Figure 2) at the distal end of centrioles. In spermatocytes, centrioles have a specific behavior as both mother and daughter centrioles of each pair elongate and dock to the plasma membrane.
evidence: The manuscript describes known behavior of centrioles in spermatocytes.

claim: All four basal bodies (BB) extend a TZ, also described as a primary cilium-like structure.
source: All four basal bodies (BB) extend a TZ, also described as a primary cilium-like structure (Figure 2A) (Pasmans and Tates, 1971; Riparbelli et al., 2012; Gottardo et al., 2013; Vieillard et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about basal body behavior in spermatocytes.

claim: During meiosis, all four basal bodies are engulfed inside the cytoplasm, together with the primary like cilium which hence creates a ciliary cap that ensheaths each basal body distal end.
source: Subsequently, during meiosis, all four basal bodies are engulfed inside the cytoplasm, together with the primary like cilium which hence creates a ciliary cap that ensheaths each basal body distal end.
evidence: The manuscript describes known developmental processes in spermatogenesis.

claim: After meiosis and at the onset of axoneme elongation, the ciliary cap is remodeled and a distinct domain, the ring centriole, appears at its base.
source: After meiosis and at the onset of axoneme elongation, the ciliary cap is remodeled and a distinct domain, the ring centriole, appears at its base (Vieillard et al., 2016; Basiri et al., 2014; Fabian and Brill, 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about ciliary cap remodeling.

claim: The axoneme grows inside the ciliary cap, which concomitantly migrates, extruding the nascent axoneme out in the cytoplasm.
source: The axoneme grows inside the ciliary cap, which concomitantly migrates, extruding the nascent axoneme out in the cytoplasm (Figure 2A) (Pasmans and Tates, 1971; Riparbelli et al., 2013; Gottardo et al., 2013).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about axoneme growth.

claim: Dzip1, Fam92 and Cby all localize at the centriolar distal ends in early spermatocytes.
source: We observed that Dzip1, Fam92 and Cby all localize at the centriolar distal ends in early spermatocytes (Figure 2B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence localization data.

claim: During centriolar/BB maturation, as the ciliary cap grows, Dzip1 and Fam92 localizations are extended and overlap with Cby.
source: During centriolar/BB maturation, as the ciliary cap grows, Dzip1 and Fam92 localizations are extended and overlap with Cby, as revealed by 3D-SIM observations (Figure 2D).
evidence: The manuscript reports super-resolution microscopy observations.

claim: In spermatids, when the TZ migrates away from the basal body, Dzip1 and Fam92 strongly accumulate with Cby at the ring centriole.
source: In spermatids, when the TZ migrates away from the basal body, we observed that Dzip1 and Fam92 strongly accumulate with Cby at the ring centriole (Figure 2B–C, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence localization data.

claim: Dzip1/Fam92/Cby interact at the ciliary transition zone.
source: Together, these results strongly indicate that Dzip1/Fam92/Cby interact at the ciliary transition zone.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional interaction from co-localization and co-IP data.

claim: dzip11 flies are viable but show typical behavioral defects associated with ciliary dysfunction in Drosophila.
source: dzip11 and fam921 flies are viable but show typical behavioral defects associated with ciliary dysfunction in Drosophila.
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations of mutant flies.

claim: fam921 flies are viable but show typical behavioral defects associated with ciliary dysfunction in Drosophila.
source: dzip11 and fam921 flies are viable but show typical behavioral defects associated with ciliary dysfunction in Drosophila.
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations of mutant flies.

claim: No dzip11 flies reached the top of the tube in geotaxis response assays.
source: Whereas most of the control flies reach and stay at the top of the tube 30 s after the bang, no dzip11 flies reached the top of the tube (Video 1).
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral assay results.

claim: dzip11/Df flies not only fail to climb, but are completely immotile with held up wings.
source: This phenotype was worsened in dzip11/Df as the flies not only fail to climb, but are completely immotile with held up wings (Video 2), indicating that dzip11 is likely not a complete null allele.
evidence: The manuscript reports behavioral phenotype observations.

claim: dzip11 is likely not a complete null allele.
source: This phenotype was worsened in dzip11/Df as the flies not only fail to climb, but are completely immotile with held up wings (Video 2), indicating that dzip11 is likely not a complete null allele.
evidence: The manuscript infers allele strength from phenotypic comparison.

claim: Both dzip11 and dzip11/Df behavioral phenotypes were fully rescued by one copy of dzip1::GFP.
source: Both dzip11 and dzip11/Df behavioral phenotypes were fully rescued by one copy of dzip1::GFP (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports rescue experiment results.

claim: 17% of fam921 flies could reach the top of the tube in geotaxis response assays.
source: In contrast, a few percentage (17%) of fam921 flies could reach the top of the tube (Figure 3A) and no differences could be observed when comparing fam921 flies and fam921 over its cognate deficiency (fam921/Df), indicating that fam921 is likely a null allele.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative behavioral assay results.

claim: fam921 is likely a null allele.
source: In contrast, a few percentage (17%) of fam921 flies could reach the top of the tube (Figure 3A) and no differences could be observed when comparing fam921 flies and fam921 over its cognate deficiency (fam921/Df), indicating that fam921 is likely a null allele.
evidence: The manuscript infers allele strength from phenotypic comparison with deficiency.

claim: The fam92::GFP rescue construct partially restores the climbing behavior of the fam921 mutant flies.
source: The fam92::GFP rescue construct partially restores the climbing behavior of the fam921 mutant flies.
evidence: The manuscript reports rescue experiment results.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 have a regulatory role in sensory cilia assembly or function.
source: These observations reveal a graded requirement for Fam92 and Dzip1 in Drosophila geotaxis response and indicate a regulatory role of this complex in sensory cilia assembly or function.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional role from behavioral phenotypes.

claim: Cilia are essentially absent in dzip11 antennal chordotonal organs.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cilia were essentially absent in dzip11 antennal chordotonal organs, but were still present in fam921 antennae (Figure 3B and F), in agreement with their milder geotaxis defect behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations.

claim: Cilia were still present in fam921 antennae.
source: Strikingly, we observed that cilia were essentially absent in dzip11 antennal chordotonal organs, but were still present in fam921 antennae (Figure 3B and F), in agreement with their milder geotaxis defect behavior.
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations.

claim: In fam921 flies, 25% of scolopidia showed reduced cilia number (one or no cilia).
source: In fam921 flies, 25% of scolopidia (total observed n = 54) showed reduced cilia number (one or no cilia).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Defects in axonemal structure were occasionally observed in fam921 flies, such as lack of microtubule doublets (6%).
source: In addition, defects in axonemal structure were occasionally observed, such as lack of microtubule doublets (Figure 3C, asterisks, 6%), excess accumulation of material beneath the ciliary membrane (arrows) and deformation of the membrane (Figure 3C, upper panel, dot, 4%).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy observations.

claim: Transition zones were completely disorganized in dzip11 antennae.
source: Transition zones were completely disorganized in dzip11 antennae as revealed by serial-cross and longitudinal sections (Figure 3D–E) and no more axoneme-to-membrane linkers could be observed.
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations.

claim: No axoneme-to-membrane linkers could be observed in dzip11 antennae.
source: Transition zones were completely disorganized in dzip11 antennae as revealed by serial-cross and longitudinal sections (Figure 3D–E) and no more axoneme-to-membrane linkers could be observed.
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations.

claim: Basal bodies were normally present at the dendrite distal tip in dzip11 antennae.
source: Basal bodies were normally present at the dendrite distal tip (Figure 3D, lower panel), but we observed a rapid disorganization of the axoneme, with its complete abrogation a few microns above the basal body (Figure 3D–E).
evidence: The manuscript reports electron microscopy observations.

claim: Loss of Dzip1 or Fam92 affects TZ assembly required for sensory cilia formation.
source: Hence, these observations demonstrate that loss of Dzip1 or Fam92 affects TZ assembly required for sensory cilia formation.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional requirement from structural defects observed by EM.

claim: There is a strong reduction of the fertility of fam921 males compared to controls.
source: We observed a strong reduction of the fertility of fam921 males compared to controls. This defect is restored by expressing Fam92-GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports fertility assay results.

claim: The fertility defect of fam921 males is restored by expressing Fam92-GFP.
source: We observed a strong reduction of the fertility of fam921 males compared to controls. This defect is restored by expressing Fam92-GFP (Figure 4A).
evidence: The manuscript reports rescue experiment results.

claim: dzip11 testes showed a marked dispersion of the nuclei along the cysts.
source: However, dzip11 testes showed a marked dispersion of the nuclei along the cysts and, as a consequence, altered migration of sperm individualization complexes (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations.

claim: dzip11 testes showed altered migration of sperm individualization complexes.
source: However, dzip11 testes showed a marked dispersion of the nuclei along the cysts and, as a consequence, altered migration of sperm individualization complexes (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations and infers consequence.

claim: Nuclear dispersion is also observed, to a lesser extent, in fam921 testes.
source: Nuclear dispersion is also observed, to a lesser extent, in fam921 testes (Figure 4B and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations.

claim: One possible origin of nuclei dispersion is defective axonemal elongation.
source: One possible origin of nuclei dispersion is defective axonemal elongation (Vieillard et al., 2016; Soulavie et al., 2014) and EM analysis confirmed that axonemes were affected in fam921 cells (Figure 4D, 125/448 broken axonemes, 25/448 missing central pair, 52/448 missing axoneme).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature and provides supporting EM data.

claim: Axonemes were affected in fam921 cells (125/448 broken axonemes, 25/448 missing central pair, 52/448 missing axoneme).
source: One possible origin of nuclei dispersion is defective axonemal elongation (Vieillard et al., 2016; Soulavie et al., 2014) and EM analysis confirmed that axonemes were affected in fam921 cells (Figure 4D, 125/448 broken axonemes, 25/448 missing central pair, 52/448 missing axoneme).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy analysis.

claim: In dzip11 testes, 6/126 broken axonemes, 1/126 missing central pair, 1/126 missing axonemes were observed.
source: As well, in dzip11 or dzip11/Df mutant testes, marked axonemal defects could be observed. In dzip11 testes, we observed 6/126 broken axonemes, 1/126 missing central pair, 1/126 missing axonemes (Figure 4C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy analysis.

claim: In very young dzip11/Df spermatid cysts, up to 60% of spermatids with missing or broken axonemes were observed.
source: More severe defects were observed in very young dzip11/Df spermatid cysts, with up to 60% of spermatids with missing or broken axonemes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy analysis.

claim: In older dzip11/Df cysts, the number of spermatids/cyst was much reduced compared to control (mean = 44 spermatids/cyst compared to control = 63.4).
source: However, in older cysts, the number of spermatids/cyst was much reduced compared to control (mean = 44 spermatids/cyst compared to control = 63.4), but almost all remaining elongated spermatids showed normal axonemes (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative electron microscopy analysis.

claim: Young spermatids with severe axonemal defects fail to elongate and are not observed in cross sections of older spermatid cysts.
source: These observations suggest that young spermatids with severe axonemal defects fail to elongate and are not observed in cross sections of older spermatid cysts.
evidence: The manuscript infers developmental outcome from quantitative observations at different stages.

claim: Fam92 and Dzip1 are necessary at the ciliary TZ for cilia formation both in sensory neurons and male germ cells.
source: Taken together, these results demonstrate that Fam92 and Dzip1 are necessary at the ciliary TZ for cilia formation both in sensory neurons and male germ cells.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes conclusions from multiple experimental observations.

claim: Cby-Tom is almost completely lost from ciliary TZ in dzip11/Df sensory neurons.
source: Cby-Tom is almost completely lost from ciliary TZ in dzip11/Df sensory neurons (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: In dzip11/Df spermatocytes, Cby-Tom signal is strongly reduced at the tip of centrioles.
source: In spermatocytes, Cby-Tom signal is strongly reduced at the tip of centrioles (Figure 5A,D) but, in rare occasions, expanded at one centriole of the pair (asterisk, 2%).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: The amount of Fam92-GFP is severely reduced in dzip11/Df sensory cilia base.
source: The amount of Fam92-GFP is severely reduced in dzip11/Df sensory cilia base (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B) and in spermatocytes (Figure 5B,D, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Dzip1 is required at the basal body/TZ to recruit or stabilize both Cby and Fam92.
source: Altogether, these observations indicate that Dzip1 is required at the basal body/TZ to recruit or stabilize both Cby and Fam92.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional requirement from localization dependencies.

claim: In fam921 mutant flies, Dzip1-GFP is slightly reduced at the distal tip of basal bodies in sensory cilia.
source: In fam921 mutant flies, Dzip1-GFP is slightly reduced at the distal tip of basal bodies in sensory cilia (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: In fam921 spermatocytes, Dzip1-GFP domain is sometimes expanded (8.3% of cases).
source: In fam921 spermatocytes, Dzip1-GFP domain is sometimes expanded (8.3% of cases, Figure 5D), but the overall Dzip1-GFP expression is also slightly reduced (Figure 5C, arrows, 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Cby-Tom is completely lost in both fam921 ciliated tissues.
source: Cby-Tom is completely lost in both fam921 ciliated tissues (Figure 5A, arrowheads and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Fam92 is required to recruit Cby, but not Dzip1, at the TZ.
source: Hence, Fam92 is required to recruit Cby, but not Dzip1, at the TZ.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional requirement from localization dependencies.

claim: In cby1 tissues, Fam92-GFP completely disappears from basal bodies.
source: As well, in cby1 tissues, Fam92-GFP completely disappears from basal bodies (Figure 5B, arrowhead and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that Cby and Fam92 stabilize each other at the basal body.
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Cby and Fam92 stabilize each other at the basal body.
source: As well, in cby1 tissues, Fam92-GFP completely disappears from basal bodies (Figure 5B, arrowhead and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B), indicating that Cby and Fam92 stabilize each other at the basal body.
evidence: The manuscript infers mutual stabilization from reciprocal localization dependencies.

claim: In cby1 mutant spermatocytes, an extended domain of Dzip1-GFP is occasionally observed (4.5%).
source: In cby1 mutant spermatocytes, an extended domain of Dzip1-GFP is occasionally observed (Figure 5C, arrows, 4.5%, 5D).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Dzip1 is required to recruit or stabilize both Fam92 and Cby at centrioles, but does not depend on Fam92 or Cby for its targeting to centrioles.
source: These observations establish a functional hierarchy for Dzip1, Fam92 and Cby: Dzip1 is required to recruit or stabilize both Fam92 and Cby at centrioles, but does not depend on Fam92 or Cby for its targeting to centrioles, the latter only restricting Dzip1 to the proximal TZ.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes functional hierarchy from multiple localization dependency experiments.

claim: Cby and Fam92 restrict Dzip1 to the proximal TZ.
source: These observations establish a functional hierarchy for Dzip1, Fam92 and Cby: Dzip1 is required to recruit or stabilize both Fam92 and Cby at centrioles, but does not depend on Fam92 or Cby for its targeting to centrioles, the latter only restricting Dzip1 to the proximal TZ.
evidence: The manuscript infers regulatory function from domain expansion phenotypes.

claim: Fam92 and Cby mutually depend on each other to localize at the TZ.
source: Conversely, Fam92 and Cby mutually depend on each other to localize at the TZ.
evidence: The manuscript synthesizes conclusion from reciprocal localization dependencies.

claim: In Drosophila, Mks1 is required to assemble the MKS complex.
source: We first investigated the behavior of Mks1, a component of the core conserved MKS complex (Weatherbee et al., 2009). In Drosophila, Mks1 is required to assemble the MKS complex, but removal of MKS components leads to only very mild defects of cilia assembly (Vieillard et al., 2016; Pratt et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about Mks1 function.

claim: Removal of MKS components leads to only very mild defects of cilia assembly in Drosophila.
source: We first investigated the behavior of Mks1, a component of the core conserved MKS complex (Weatherbee et al., 2009). In Drosophila, Mks1 is required to assemble the MKS complex, but removal of MKS components leads to only very mild defects of cilia assembly (Vieillard et al., 2016; Pratt et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about MKS complex function.

claim: In dzip11/Df and fam921 mutant flies, Mks1-GFP is lost or reduced at the TZ in both ciliated tissues.
source: In dzip11/Df and fam921 mutant flies, Mks1-GFP is lost or reduced at the TZ in both ciliated tissues (Figure 6A, arrows, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 are important for the recruitment or stabilization of the MKS module at the TZ.
source: Dzip1 and Fam92 are hence important for the recruitment or stabilization of the MKS module at the TZ.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional requirement from localization dependency.

claim: Cep290 is a core conserved TZ component which plays a prominent role in TZ assembly in many organisms, including Drosophila.
source: Cep290 is a core conserved TZ component which plays a prominent role in TZ assembly in many organisms, including Drosophila (Craige et al., 2010; Rachel et al., 2015; Li et al., 2016a; Basiri et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about Cep290 function.

claim: In flies, Cep290 is located at the base of the TZ in sensory neurons.
source: In flies, Cep290 is located at the base of the TZ in sensory neurons and is a critical component of the migrating ring centriole during spermatogenesis (Basiri et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about Cep290 localization.

claim: Cep290 is a critical component of the migrating ring centriole during spermatogenesis.
source: In flies, Cep290 is located at the base of the TZ in sensory neurons and is a critical component of the migrating ring centriole during spermatogenesis (Basiri et al., 2014).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about Cep290 function.

claim: In the absence of Dzip1, Cep290-GFP shows expanded domains, both in spermatocytes and in Ch neurons.
source: In the absence of Dzip1, besides a small but significant reduction of Cep290-GFP on spermatocyte centrioles, we observed striking Cep290-GFP expanded domains, both in spermatocytes and in Ch neurons (Figure 6A–B, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Around 13% of centrioles in spermatocytes and a majority in antennae showed an expanded Cep290-GFP domain in dzip1 mutants.
source: Around 13% of centrioles in spermatocytes and a majority in antennae showed an expanded Cep290-GFP domain (Figure 6A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: In fam921 mutants, a few Cep290-GFP expanded domains were observed in spermatocytes and antennae, but with no significant difference in overall Cep290-GFP intensity.
source: In fam921 mutants, we also observed a few Cep290-GFP expanded domains in spermatocytes and antennae, but with no significant difference in overall Cep290-GFP intensity (Figure 6A–B, arrows).
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative immunofluorescence observations.

claim: cep2900153-G4 mutant shows severe uncoordination.
source: This mutant shows severe uncoordination and completely disorganized spermatid cysts with dispersed nuclei (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), which is a consequence of the severe axonemal elongation defects observed in this mutant (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports phenotypic observations.

claim: cep2900153-G4 mutant shows completely disorganized spermatid cysts with dispersed nuclei.
source: This mutant shows severe uncoordination and completely disorganized spermatid cysts with dispersed nuclei (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A), which is a consequence of the severe axonemal elongation defects observed in this mutant (not shown).
evidence: The manuscript reports microscopy observations.

claim: The phenotypes of cep2900153-G4 were completely rescued by two copies of cep290::GFP.
source: The phenotypes were completely rescued by two copies of cep290::GFP (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports rescue experiment results.

claim: In cep2900153-G4 flies, Dzip1 and Fam92 are strongly reduced or lost at the TZ, both in spermatocytes and in sensory neurons.
source: We observed that in cep2900153-G4 flies, Dzip1 and Fam92 are strongly reduced or lost at the TZ, both in spermatocytes (Figure 6C) and in sensory neurons (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: The manuscript reports immunofluorescence observations.

claim: Cep290 is required during TZ assembly to recruit Dzip1 and Fam92.
source: These observations demonstrate that Cep290 is required during TZ assembly to recruit Dzip1 and Fam92, which in turn restrict Cep290 scaffolding to the proximal part of the TZ.
evidence: The manuscript infers functional requirement from localization dependencies.

claim: Dzip1 and Fam92 restrict Cep290 scaffolding to the proximal part of the TZ.
source: These observations demonstrate that Cep290 is required during TZ assembly to recruit Dzip1 and Fam92, which in turn restrict Cep290 scaffolding to the proximal part of the TZ.
evidence: The manuscript infers regulatory function from domain expansion phenotypes.

claim: Defects in BB anchoring to the plasma membrane in spermatocytes lead to aberrant growth of axonemal microtubules.
source: Defects in BB anchoring to the plasma membrane in spermatocytes lead to aberrant growth of axonemal microtubules (Vieillard et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about BB anchoring defects.

claim: CG6652-GFP only labels axonemal microtubules in flies.
source: We used the specific axonemal marker CG6652-GFP that only labels axonemal microtubules in flies (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C–D).
evidence: The manuscript reports marker specificity validated by control experiments.

claim: Aberrant growth of axonemal microtubules was observed in spermatocytes, with graded severities increasing from fam921, dzip11 to cep2900153-G4 mutant flies.
source: With this marker, we observed aberrant growth of axonemal microtubules in spermatocytes, with graded severities increasing from fam921, dzip11 to cep2900153-G4 mutant flies (Figure 7A–B).
evidence: The manuscript reports comparative microscopy observations.

claim: 30% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in fam921 testes.
source: 30% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in fam921 testes, 34% in dzip11/Df and 76% in cep2900153-G4.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative microscopy analysis.

claim: 34% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in dzip11/Df testes.
source: 30% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in fam921 testes, 34% in dzip11/Df and 76% in cep2900153-G4.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative microscopy analysis.

claim: 76% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in cep2900153-G4 testes.
source: 30% of centrioles showed CG6652 extensions in fam921 testes, 34% in dzip11/Df and 76% in cep2900153-G4.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative microscopy analysis.

claim: In fam921 testes, 96% of the centriole pairs present microtubule extensions on only one centriole.
source: More strikingly, whereas 68% of the centriole pairs present extensions from both centrioles in cep2900153-G4 spermatocytes, we observed that in fam921 testes, 96% of the centriole pairs present microtubule extensions on only one centriole.
evidence: The manuscript reports quantitative microscopy analysis.

claim: The asymmetric penetrance of the phenotype in fam921 is related to centriole age.
source: This asymmetric penetrance of the phenotype is related to centriole age. Indeed, among 24 centriole pairs for which mother and daughter identities could be unequivocally assigned, 19 daughter centrioles (79%) and only five mother centrioles (21%) were affected.
evidence: The manuscript infers relationship from quantitative analysis of centriole identity.

claim: Among 24 centriole pairs in fam921 for which mother and daughter identities could be unequivocally assigned, 19 daughter centrioles (79%) and only five mother centrioles (21%) were affected.

evidence: The manuscript cites established literature about mammalian centriole capping.

claim: There are no clear evidence in Drosophila that CP110 or CEP97 need to or are specifically removed before axonemal elongation.
source: However, there are no clear evidence in Drosophila that these proteins need to or are specifically removed before axonemal elongation (Galletta et al., 2016; Franz et al., 2013; Delgehyr et al., 2012).
evidence: The manuscript cites literature showing lack of evidence for removal requirement in Drosophila.

claim: Regulation of axonemal assembly and cell cycle regulation are tightly linked in dividing spermatocytes.
source: Our observations indicate that regulation of axonemal assembly and cell cycle regulation are tightly linked in these dividing cells, but the effectors of this control still need to be identified.
evidence: The manuscript infers linkage from timing observations.
